title: All Have Sinned; Righteousness Through Faith
summary: Paul answers objections: the Jews' advantage is real, since they were entrusted with God's words, and human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness. Then he draws a chain of Old Testament quotations into a verdict: Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, and no one will be justified by works of the law. But now God's righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, whom God presented as the atoning sacrifice, so that he is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.
story: This is the turning point of the letter's first half. Since 1:18 Paul has been building a case: the Gentile world suppressed the truth (chapter 1), and the Jew who had the law did not keep it (chapter 2). Verses 1-20 close that case with the whole world silenced and accountable to God. Then verse 21 opens with two small words, “But now”, and the letter turns from diagnosis to remedy. Verses 21-26 are among the most compressed and important sentences Paul ever wrote, and much of the rest of Romans explains them. Chapter 4 will show that Abraham himself was justified this way.
historical:
Paul's debate partner in verses 1-8 voices objections that Paul's preaching had actually provoked. Verse 8 says some slanderously claimed Paul taught that people should do evil so that good might come. That charge, that grace encourages sin, followed Paul throughout his ministry, and he answers it at length in chapter 6. Paul's letters show that he was accused both by Jewish opponents and by some Jewish Christians of undermining the law, which is why the chapter ends with his insistence that faith upholds the law.

The phrase works of the law (verses 20, 28) sits at the center of a modern debate. The Reformation tradition, from Martin Luther and John Calvin onward, generally read it as any human effort to earn God's favor by obeying his commands. Since E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977), many scholars have argued that Judaism in Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation but of grace and covenant, with obedience as the response to grace; James Dunn and N. T. Wright argued that works of the law refers especially to the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and the Sabbath. Critics of this new perspective reply that Paul's argument in verses 19-20 and in 4:4-5 concerns human doing in general, not only boundary markers. Many interpreters now hold that both concerns are present.
cultural:
Verse 25 uses the word hilasterion, which the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) uses for the mercy seat, the gold cover of the ark of the covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15). A reader steeped in the Scriptures would hear an image of the place where God met his people and dealt with their sin. Paul says God presented Christ publicly as that place, not hidden in the inner room of the temple but displayed.

Redemption (verse 24) was also a familiar word. It named the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner, and in the Old Testament it described God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Justify (dikaioo) came from the lawcourt: it means to declare someone in the right, to acquit. Paul joins images from the courtroom, the slave market, and the temple to describe one act of God in Christ.
literary: The chapter falls into three parts. Verses 1-8 are a rapid exchange of questions and answers, with objections twice met by “Certainly not!” (verses 4 and 6), a strong Greek negative that Paul uses repeatedly in Romans. Verses 9-20 are a catena, a chain of Scripture quotations drawn from the Psalms (14, 53, 5, 140, 10, 36) and Isaiah 59, arranged to move from the whole person to throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, and eyes, until every part of human life is covered. Verses 21-26 are a single dense statement whose key words (righteousness, faith, grace, redemption, blood, demonstrate) repeat and interlock. Verses 27-31 return to questions and answers and draw the consequences: boasting is excluded, God is the God of Gentiles too, and the law is upheld.

outline.t: God's righteousness revealed through faith in Christ
No boasting, one God, and the law upheld

doctrines.note: Paul concludes that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, and that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Sin is universal and it is a power people are under, not merely a set of mistakes.
God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness. God does not overlook sin; he deals with it himself in Christ, so that he is just in forgiving.

People are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Justification is God's declaration that the ungodly are in the right with him, received as a gift, not earned.
Righteousness comes through faith, to all who believe, without distinction. Faith excludes boasting because it receives rather than achieves, and the same faith puts Jew and Gentile on equal footing.

words.note: Dikaioo, to justify, to declare or put in the right. It is a courtroom word. Protestant tradition has stressed that it declares a verdict rather than describing a gradual change; Catholic tradition has held that God's declaration also makes the person righteous. Some recent scholars add that the verdict includes membership in God's covenant people. It appears six times in this chapter, beginning in verse 4, where it is used of God himself being proved right.

Hilasterion, the place or means of atonement. Scholars have debated whether it means propitiation (turning away God's wrath, argued by Leon Morris), expiation (wiping away sin, argued by C. H. Dodd), or the mercy seat itself. Since the context speaks of God's wrath (1:18) and of sins passed over, many hold that both removing sin and satisfying God's justice are in view.

Pistis, faith, trust. In verse 22 the phrase translated faith in Jesus Christ can also be rendered the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and scholars are divided. The first reading stresses the believer's trust in Christ; the second stresses Christ's own faithful obedience to death. Both readings affirm that believers are justified by trusting him.

Apolutrosis, redemption, release by payment of a price. It recalls the freeing of slaves and God's redemption of Israel from Egypt. Paul says the redemption is in Christ Jesus: he is the one in whom release is found.

christ: Verses 21-26 place Christ at the center of the whole problem Paul has described. God presented him as the atoning sacrifice through his blood. In his death, God deals with human sin in a way that shows his own righteousness: he neither excuses sin nor abandons sinners. He is “just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.” The Old Testament sacrifices, the mercy seat, and the Day of Atonement all find their meaning here; Paul says this righteousness is attested by the Law and the Prophets. The one who fulfilled what they pointed to is not an idea but a person, Jesus, whose death in history is the place where God met humanity's plight.

hard.q: If God simply forgives, why was the death of Jesus necessary?
hard.a:
Paul's answer in verses 25-26 is that God had passed over sins in his forbearance, and this raised a question about his justice. A judge who simply let the guilty go would not be just. The cross demonstrates God's righteousness: it shows that sin is serious enough to require a costly remedy, and that God himself provides it.

Christians have described how this works in several ways. Penal substitution, emphasized in the Reformation tradition, holds that Christ bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners. Other traditions stress Christ's victory over the powers of sin and death, his perfect obedience offered to the Father, or the cross as the ultimate demonstration of God's love. Most theologians see these as complementary rather than rival pictures, though they differ over which is central. Some modern critics have objected that a punishment borne by an innocent person is itself unjust; defenders reply that the one who bears it is not a third party but God himself in the person of the Son, freely giving himself. The church's shared confession is that Christ died for our sins and that salvation is God's own act of grace.

questions: Paul's list of quotations moves from the throat to the feet. Which part of that description do you find hardest to admit applies to you?
Why does Paul say that faith excludes boasting? How does the way you think you are accepted by God shape how you treat others?
“There is no distinction”, Paul says: all have sinned, and all are justified the same way. What difference would it make if churches truly believed that?
